messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

At 52, he still remembers the accident in the body before he can put it into words. He is a European man, long accustomed to being the one who keeps a set moving, who can assess a room quickly and make a hundred decisions without showing strain. For years, work as a film director has rewarded that part of him: the careful eye, the ability to stay calm under pressure, the instinct to anticipate what might go wrong before anyone else notices. He has lived for control, in a profession that depends on it.

The accident happens on a remote location during a night shoot, when the production has already run long and everyone is tired. He is riding in a vehicle between setups, talking through the next scene in his head, when everything changes in an instant. The crash is violent and sudden, metal and glass and noise. He does not initially understand what has happened; he experiences it as a sequence of sensations that do not yet make sense. There is the impact, the sharp smell of fuel, a flash of pain, and then the terrifying recognition that he may not be able to move. He believes he is dying. He remembers calling out, though he is not sure whether he is calling for help or simply trying to remind himself that he is still there.

In the aftermath, he is physically injured, but the deeper wound is the knowledge that his body can fail him without warning. During the first days and weeks, he cannot stop replaying the moment of impact. He wakes with a jolt, already braced for the sound of breaking metal. At night he sees the accident in fragments: the angle of the headlights, the tilt of the road, the second before everything spins. He avoids driving whenever possible and becomes tense as soon as he is a passenger, his eyes fixed ahead, jaw tight, one hand gripping the seat or the door handle. Even in ordinary traffic, he scans for danger with a force that exhausts him.

He returns to work because he does not know how not to. From the outside, he remains composed, efficient, and exacting. On set, he still gives clear instructions and solves problems quickly, but his concentration is not as steady as it once was. He startles at loud noises, especially sudden metal bangs, slamming doors, or the shriek of equipment being moved. His body reacts before his mind catches up. He notices himself flinching and feels embarrassed by it, annoyed that something so old and familiar as a film set can now leave him on edge. He becomes more controlling in subtle ways, checking safety details repeatedly, watching the movements of crew members, needing to know exactly who is where and what is happening. He tells himself he is simply being thorough, though part of him understands that he is trying to keep dread from finding a way in.

At home, his relationship has become a place where his fear is most visible. His partner notices that he is less patient, more distant, and often preoccupied. He has trouble describing what he feels because the experience is so physical—tight chest, shallow breath, a sense of being trapped in his own skin. He sometimes becomes irritable over small things, then withdraws and grows quiet with shame. He is not used to being comforted, and when his partner reaches for him at night, he may tense first before relaxing, as if even care must be assessed for danger.

He also finds himself increasingly aware of his own mortality in ways that feel intrusive and unwelcome. A routine ache can make him wonder if something is wrong. A detour on a road can trigger a wave of panic so quickly that he must pull over and wait for it to pass. He avoids talking about the accident, especially the moment when he thought he was not going to survive, because naming it seems to bring back the helplessness attached to it. Yet in quieter moments he admits that the event has changed the way he moves through the world. He is still directing films, still making decisions, still showing up, but there is now a constant strain beneath the surface, as though some part of him remains in that crushed vehicle, listening for rescue and not fully convinced it will come.
